checkpoints: Storing the full HTML as a plain text column inline in the same row as url/host/statusCode means each row's size is dominated by the page body rather than the small metadata fields.
Once a text value exceeds roughly 2 KB, Postgres moves it out-of-line into TOAST storage, which bloats the table's physical footprint and skews the query planner's row-width statistics.

Because TOAST bloat and skewed statistics affect the whole table, metadata-only queries such as listing pages or looking up by host slow down even though they never select htmlBody, since they still scan a table whose rows are secretly huge.

Separating the heavy blob from the hot metadata fixes the root cause: push the raw HTML to object storage such as S3 or MinIO under a key derived from the page (e.g. a hash of the URL or a UUID), and keep only a content digest plus that object key in the page row alongside url/host/statusCode/contentType.
A content digest — a hash of the HTML body — doubles as a cheap way to detect duplicate or unchanged pages without re-reading the full HTML on every crawl.

With the blob moved out, the write path still upserts a small metadata row as before, but the body write goes through an object-storage put call instead of populating htmlBody, so a metadata scan now touches a table of small, fixed-width-ish rows with no TOAST involvement.

Inline text storage is not inherently wrong and is genuinely fine at demo or small scale; the trade-off only tips toward object storage at billions of rows, where the extra network hop to fetch the body when actually needed (rendering, re-parsing, re-indexing) and the added consistency burden between Postgres and the object store are worth paying to keep the frequently-queried metadata table small and fast.

The migration's benefit can be verified concretely by comparing metadata-query latency and table-plus-TOAST size before and after the change, and by confirming the HTML is still retrievable end-to-end through its stored object key.

The `enqueue` method issues `BF.EXISTS`, `BF.ADD`, and `zadd` as three separate awaited Redis calls with no atomicity between them, so two workers enqueuing the same brand-new URL can both read the membership check as a miss before either has run `BF.ADD`, and both then push the URL onto the ZSET as a duplicate.

Each enqueue on this path pays three sequential network round trips to Redis (one for the existence check, one for the bloom add, one for the queue add), and because each awaited call must finish before the next starts, that round-trip count directly caps how many URLs the frontier can accept per second.

The check-and-set can be made atomic and single-round-trip by fusing `BF.EXISTS`, `BF.ADD`, and `zadd` into one Lua script and registering it as a custom ioredis command (for example via `redis.defineCommand`), since Redis runs a Lua script as one atomic, single-threaded server-side operation.

Because the fused script runs as a single atomic unit, no second worker can observe the bloom filter mid-check, which closes the double-add race entirely, and replacing three awaited calls with one round trip raises enqueue throughput roughly 10x.

Bloom-filter dedup for a crawler is inherently best-effort, so an occasional double-enqueued brand-new URL is generally harmless — the Lua-script fuse is worth making specifically when exactly-once enqueue semantics are required or the system is throughput-bound on enqueue, not as a default change to every code path.

Correctness of the fix can be verified by concurrently calling enqueue with the same brand-new URL from many clients and asserting the queue's size grows by exactly one instead of accumulating duplicate entries.

The throughput claim can be verified by benchmarking enqueues-per-second on the original three-call sequential path versus the single fused Lua-script call, comparing the numbers before and after the change.

`this.redis.get(cacheKey)` has the return type `string | null`, where `null` signals a genuine cache miss (the key was never set, or its TTL expired) while an empty string `""` is a legitimate cached value.
An empty robots.txt body is a meaningful, valid result — it means "no restrictions apply" — so storing it in the cache as `""` is correct behavior, not an edge case that needs to be filtered out.

In JavaScript, empty strings are falsy, so a truthiness check like `if (cached)` cannot tell apart "nothing was cached" (`null`) from "an empty value was cached" (`""`) — both fall through to the same branch.

Because the cache-hit branch tests truthiness instead of `cached !== null`, a host whose robots.txt is empty makes every request fall into the else branch, refetch `/robots.txt`, and overwrite the cache with the same empty string, even though the previous write's 60-second TTL was still valid.

The TTL itself and the `redis.set` call both behave correctly; the defect is entirely on the read side — the cached value is never successfully recognized as a hit for these hosts, so it always looks like a miss.

Hosts whose robots.txt content is non-empty never trigger the bug, since any non-empty string is truthy, which is why the failure hides silently and only affects a specific subset of hosts rather than breaking the cache uniformly.

Replacing the truthiness check with an explicit presence check, `cached !== null`, fixes the bug by treating "a value was returned from Redis" as the cache-hit signal, regardless of whether that value happens to be an empty string.

The fix can be verified by seeding the same host's empty robots.txt twice within the 60-second TTL window and confirming `fakeFetch`/robots.txt fires only once, or by checking the Redis TTL on `crawler:robots:<host>:body` to confirm the key is being read rather than repeatedly overwritten.

The enqueue path never calls `BF.RESERVE` before issuing `BF.EXISTS`/`BF.ADD`, so RedisBloom auto-creates the `seen:urls` filter on the very first bloom command it sees, using its own built-in defaults rather than any values configured in the service.

RedisBloom's default sizing for an auto-created filter is roughly a 0.01 error rate and a capacity of exactly one hundred items — which is why the frontier stalls right around the hundred-URL mark rather than at some arbitrary point.

Once real inserts exceed a bloom filter's reserved capacity, its actual false-positive rate climbs well past the advertised rate, so `BF.EXISTS` starts reporting brand-new URLs as already seen and the crawler wrongly discards them as duplicates.

A bloom filter has exactly one failure mode — the false positive — and returning a false positive is normal, non-error behavior; nothing throws or logs, so the frontier silently stops accepting most URLs instead of surfacing an error.

The fix is to explicitly call `BF.RESERVE(key, errorRate, capacity)` with the real configured values on module init (or lazily before the first enqueue), sizing capacity to roughly 1.5x the expected number of unique URLs to leave headroom for growth.

`BF.RESERVE` throws if the target key already exists, so the reserve call must be wrapped in a try/catch that swallows only the "item exists" error — this makes the reserve idempotent across restarts, re-asserting the correct configuration without wiping out dedup state a previous instance already built.

The fix can be verified by checking `BF.INFO` to confirm the filter's reported capacity matches the configured value instead of the silent default of one hundred, then enqueuing well past a hundred distinct URLs and confirming none of them are rejected as false duplicates.
A dangling node in PageRank is one with out-degree zero — it has no outlinks at all, so under the bare recurrence its rank mass has nowhere to flow.

In this loop, the inner accumulation `for (const v of inLinks.get(u) ?? [])` only gathers rank FROM other nodes' inlinks; there is no separate step anywhere that collects a dangling node's rank and redistributes it back across the graph.

Because dangling mass is never redistributed, the sum of the `rank` map drifts below 1 after every pass of the `for (let it = 0; it < MAX_ITERATIONS; it++)` loop, and the resulting rank ordering becomes unstable across iterations.

The fix is to compute, each iteration before building `newRank`, a `danglingSum` equal to the sum of `rank.get(u)` over every node whose `outDegree` is zero, then derive `danglingShare = (DAMPING * danglingSum) / N` and add that share to every node alongside the existing `teleport = (1 - DAMPING) / N` term so the rank vector re-normalizes to sum to 1.

This bug is dangerous precisely because the code still runs to completion and returns superficially plausible numbers; the decay only becomes visible on a real corpus containing dead-end pages, which is why it slips past shallow or toy-graph tests.

In code review, the tell is structural rather than a runtime error: there is no variable resembling `danglingSum` or `danglingShare` anywhere near the main iteration loop, signaling the redistribution step was simply never written.

A regression test for this class of bug should assert that `[...rank.values()].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)` stays approximately 1 after every single iteration, run against a graph that deliberately includes at least one dangling node so the faulty path is actually exercised.

The missing correction is conceptually the same kind of uniform redistribution as the teleport term — both `teleport` and `danglingShare` add a flat amount to every node per iteration, so omitting the dangling term is easy to overlook since the code superficially resembles a correct damped power-iteration implementation.
